inline.alt: Thousands of pilgrims at Mount Arafat during Hajj.
inline.caption: Pilgrims at Mount Arafat. Standing there from noon until sunset is the central rite of Hajj.
Golden light on desert hills. Badr lay on a caravan route in the Arabian desert; the photograph does not show Badr.
The arched ruins of an old stone building. The photograph is not of a site named in this article.

inline.alt: Aerial view of the Grand Mosque in Mecca in daylight.
inline.caption: The Grand Mosque in Mecca from the air. The Prophet ﷺ entered the city in 8 AH and granted an amnesty to most of its people.
A Roman arch at Side on the south coast of Turkey, in the region Paul travelled through.
The ruins of Perge in Turkey. Paul and Barnabas passed through Perge on their first journey (Acts 13:13, 14:25).

inline.alt: Close-up of a Bible page showing scripture text and verses.
inline.caption: An open Bible; the page shown is from Genesis. In Matthew 5:17 to 18 Jesus says that not one stroke of the Law will pass away until all is accomplished.
A rock-cut tomb in a rugged desert landscape. Rock-cut tombs of this kind are the setting scholars link with Thamud.
The Obelisk Tomb at Petra, Jordan. Ad and Iram have not been securely placed on any map, and the sites travellers photograph, like this one, belong to later peoples.

inline.alt: Aerial view of Masjid al-Haram and the Kaaba in Mecca with pilgrims gathered for prayer.
inline.caption: Masjid al-Haram and the Kaaba from the air. The Quran's chapter of the Elephant recalls an army that marched on Mecca.
A globe turned to the Eurasian continent. Most Muslims live in Asia and not in the Arab world.
A vintage globe with a sepia world map behind it. The projections point to Muslims and Christians reaching parity in the next decades.

inline.alt: Rows of worshippers inside Baitul Mukarram Mosque in Dhaka, viewed from above.
inline.caption: Worshippers in rows inside Baitul Mukarram Mosque in Dhaka, Bangladesh. The world's Muslim population grew by 347 million in a single decade.

featured.alt: A single folio of an early Quran manuscript in the Khalili Collection.
featured.caption: A folio of an early Quran. Quran 3:81 speaks of a covenant God took from the prophets.

inline.alt: A page of an early Quran manuscript in the Khalili Collection.
inline.caption: An early Quran leaf. The commentators read the messenger of 3:81 as the one who confirms what the prophets held.

inline.alt: A 1910 photograph of the Aleppo Codex at a page of Deuteronomy.
inline.caption: The Aleppo Codex, photographed in 1910. Deuteronomy 18:18 promises a prophet like Moses.

featured.alt: A decorated Quran manuscript copied by Ahmad Neyrizi in the eighteenth century.
featured.caption: A Quran copied by Ahmad Neyrizi. Quran 10:94 tells the Prophet to ask those who read the scripture before him.

inline.id: File:ISS-65 Mediterranean Sea and Gulf of Suez moonglint.jpg
inline.alt: The Gulf of Suez and the Mediterranean photographed from the International Space Station.
inline.caption: The Gulf of Suez seen from orbit. The verse comes at the end of the story of Moses, Pharaoh and the sea.

inline.id: File:Iran, tafis (commentario al corano) di tabari (in persiano), 1210-25 ca. (bnf).jpg
inline.alt: A page of a Persian translation of al-Tabari's commentary on the Quran, about 1210 to 1225.
inline.caption: A Persian version of al-Tabari's commentary, early thirteenth century. Al-Tabari's reports name Abdullah ibn Salam among those who could be asked.

featured.alt: The leaves of the Birmingham Quran manuscript in early Hijazi script.
featured.caption: The Birmingham Quran leaves, radiocarbon dated to the first decades of Islam. The Prophet dictated the Quran to scribes.

inline.alt: A single leaf of the Birmingham Quran manuscript.
inline.caption: A leaf of the Birmingham manuscript. Early copies fit the account of written pieces gathered after the Prophet.

inline.id: File:Vatican, Apostolic Library Ms Hanna Papyrus 1 - Papyrus Bodmer XIV–XV (Papyrus 75) fol 1B9r Luke 14, 3-14.jpg
inline.alt: A page of Papyrus 75 with Luke 14.
inline.caption: Papyrus 75, about 200, at Luke 14. The Gospels carry no chain of named narrators back to Jesus.

featured.alt: A Tyrian half-shekel coin of the Second Temple period.
featured.caption: A Tyrian half shekel. Exodus 30 calls the half-shekel census payment a ransom for each life.

inline.alt: A page of the Latin text of Codex Bezae at Matthew 21:46 to 22:11, from the 1899 facsimile.
inline.caption: Codex Bezae, a Gospel book of about 400. Mark 10:45 speaks of a ransom for many.

inline.alt: A Mughal painting of about 1585 of a ram with a gold chain.
inline.caption: A ram, painted in Mughal India. The sacrifice at the Hajj recalls the ram that ransomed Abraham's son (37:107).

featured.alt: A page of the 1868 printed edition of Codex Vaticanus, with Matthew 1:22 to 2:18 in Greek capitals.
featured.caption: Codex Vaticanus at Matthew 2, in its 1868 edition. Matthew reads the older prophets as fulfilled in Jesus.

inline.alt: A page of the Aleppo Codex, a Hebrew Bible in three columns.
inline.caption: The Aleppo Codex, a Hebrew Bible of the 900s. Daniel turns Jeremiah's seventy years into seventy weeks of years.

inline.alt: A Hebrew scroll of Esther on vellum, about 1850, in the Cleveland Museum of Art.
inline.caption: A Hebrew scroll. The Habakkuk commentary from Qumran, also a scroll, says the prophet did not know when the end would come.

inline.alt: A page of Codex Washingtonianus at Mark 14:29 to 40, from the 1912 facsimile.
inline.caption: Codex Washingtonianus at Mark 14. Matthew and Luke took over most of Mark and rewrote it.
inline.artist: Freer Gallery of Art, facsimile of 1912

featured.alt: A page of Codex Washingtonianus, a Greek Gospel book of about 400, from the 1912 facsimile.
featured.caption: Codex Washingtonianus, about 400, a copy of the four Gospels. The four Gospels name no author in their own text.
featured.artist: Freer Gallery of Art, facsimile of 1912

inline.alt: A page of the Latin text of Codex Bezae at John 7:8 to 22, from the 1899 facsimile.
inline.caption: Codex Bezae carries many readings found in no other manuscript.

inline.alt: A page of Codex Washingtonianus at Mark 16:12 to 17, from the 1912 facsimile.
inline.caption: Codex Washingtonianus at Mark 16. It adds a passage after 16:14 that no other Greek manuscript has.
inline.artist: Freer Gallery of Art, facsimile of 1912

featured.alt: The decorated opening page of a Hebrew Pentateuch printed in 1505.
featured.caption: A Hebrew Torah, printed in 1505. In Abu Dawud 4449 the Prophet set the Torah on a cushion and said he believed in it.

inline.alt: A page of the Aleppo Codex, a Hebrew Bible in three columns.
inline.caption: The Aleppo Codex, a Hebrew Bible of the 900s. The parallel accounts tell of a hand placed over the verse of stoning.

inline.alt: A painting of a crowded synagogue interior by Alessandro Magnasco, about 1730.
inline.caption: A synagogue, painted by Magnasco. The report shows a Torah in Jewish hands in Medina. It cannot show that the whole text was intact.

featured.alt: A Quran folio of the 800s written in gold Kufic script on parchment.
featured.caption: A Quran folio of the 800s. Quran 33:40 calls Muhammad the seal of the prophets.

inline.alt: A lithograph of about 1820 showing the Kaaba and the Sacred Mosque with Mecca behind.
inline.caption: Mecca in a lithograph of about 1820. Quran 5:3 was revealed at Arafat, outside Mecca, during the Farewell Pilgrimage.

inline.alt: A Quran folio of the 800s in Kufic script, probably from Egypt.
inline.caption: A Quran page in Kufic script. The Quran calls itself the guardian over the books before it.

inline.alt: A woodcut by Jost Amman of a brickmaker shaping bricks.
inline.caption: A brickmaker at work. The Prophet compared himself to the last brick that completes a house.
